c1.story:
Warren Buffett once joked that if a farsighted capitalist had been present at Kitty Hawk, he would have done his successors a huge favour by shooting Orville Wright down. Indian aviation has spent two decades proving the joke right. Kingfisher collapsed in 2012. Jet Airways stopped flying in 2019. Go First filed for insolvency in 2023. Air India was a loss-making ward of the state for years before the Tatas bought it back.

And yet one airline stands out. IndiGo, founded by Rahul Bhatia and Rakesh Gangwal, did the boring things relentlessly: one aircraft family, densely packed seats, planes turned around fast and flown most of the day, tickets sold online, every extra charged. Over the years it became so large and so cheap to run that it now carries most of India's domestic passengers. That is why this sector is unusual. When you buy Indian aviation through listed stocks, you are mostly buying one company.

Behind the other doors, the picture changes completely. SpiceJet, the sub-scale airline, has spent years in court with lessors, staff and former owners, its fleet partly grounded, its survival funded by promoters and new investors. Buying it is not a bet on India flying more; it is a bet on a rescue succeeding. The charter and helicopter operators, like Global Vectra flying helicopters to offshore oil rigs, live on contracts with oil companies and governments, with small fleets and lumpy earnings. And the drone companies are betting that a loosening rulebook turns a few paying customers into many.

In Indian aviation, the sector's growth and one company's profit are almost the same thing.

Air India and Akasa, the two other serious domestic carriers, are unlisted. So the listed universe gives you a near-monopoly leader, a distressed challenger, and a fringe of niche operators. Know which one you are holding.
c1.read:
The four tiles are the four doors. Read each top to bottom, then compare the bars.

  • The name and line under it tell you how the business makes money: cost per seat at scale, survival on outside funding, hourly or contract charters, or selling drone data and services.
  • The tickers show how thin the listed universe is. Each door has one or two names, and the first door has exactly one. Click a ticker to open its stock page.
  • The bar shows how much profit the company keeps. Two doors sit at medium, the scale low-cost airline and the charter operators. Two sit at low, the sub-scale airline and the drones. Notice that even the best airline in the country only reaches medium. That is not a slight on IndiGo; it is a statement about the industry, where aircraft makers, lessors, oil companies and airports are paid before the airline is.
  • The last line is the bet: travel growth landing with the lowest-cost carrier, a rescue, corporate and offshore contracts, or a rulebook that keeps loosening.

The analogy below, four kinds of bus and taxi operator, captures the gap between door one and door two. The so-what line is the key takeaway: you are buying a near-monopoly on a thin margin, not a sector. Before you read anything else, ask whether a name is the leader, a rescue or a niche, because they respond to the same news in opposite ways.

c2.story:
Picture the industry as a kitchen with five stations, and notice how little of it the airline owns.

Station one is the aircraft and its engines. Planes are ordered years ahead from Airbus or Boeing, powered by engines from Pratt and Whitney or CFM, and usually not owned at all: they are leased from Irish, Chinese, Japanese and now a few Indian lessors. When Pratt and Whitney found a manufacturing flaw in its new-generation engines in 2023, dozens of Indian narrowbodies were grounded in rotation for inspections, and the airlines could do nothing but wait.

Station two is fuel. Aviation turbine fuel is bought from Indian Oil, BPCL and HPCL, priced off global crude and taxed by each state where the plane fills up. Station three is the airport: landing, parking and passenger fees, the slots that decide when you may fly, and the airspace, managed by the state. When Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian carriers in the spring of 2025, westbound flights had to route around it, burning more fuel and in some cases adding a stop.

Station four is the airline itself: crew, scheduling, selling tickets and the obsessive art of turning a plane around in well under an hour. Station five is maintenance and the passenger: heavy checks and engine overhauls mostly done in Singapore, the Gulf or Europe, and tickets sold through MakeMyTrip or the airline's own app.

So the airline stands at one station and controls none of the others. It pays Airbus and the lessors in dollars, the oil companies at whatever crude costs, the airports at regulated rates, and the overhaul shops abroad, again in dollars. Then it sells tickets in rupees to passengers who compare every fare online. What is left is its margin.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, then the band row beneath them.

The boxes run from aircraft and engines to maintenance and the passenger. Each tells you what happens and who stands there. Notice how many foreign names appear: Airbus, Boeing, engine makers, overseas lessors, foreign overhaul shops, Gulf carriers. Aviation is the most dollar-denominated kitchen on this page.

The band row shows who holds each station. Only one cell, the airline, is coloured as India listed. The first, Airbus, Boeing and the lessors, is marked as a rival station, because those suppliers capture much of the industry's value. The oil companies, the airport operators and the foreign overhaul shops and online agents fill the rest.

The rival line is worth reading closely. It names two competitors, not one: the Gulf carriers on international routes, who connect Indian passengers to the world through Dubai, Doha and Abu Dhabi, and Air India at home, unlisted but now private and rebuilding.

  • An engine defect or delivery delay starts at station one and caps how many seats the airline can fly.
  • A crude spike starts at station two and hits margins within a quarter.
  • An airport tariff order or airspace closure starts at station three.

The note adds the two facts that frame everything: slots at the three biggest airports are the scarcest asset, and almost every cost is in dollars while almost every ticket is in rupees. The so-what line finishes the thought: the margin is whatever is left after the first three stations have been paid.

c3.story:
Who fills an Indian airliner? Mostly people paying their own money, which is the first thing to understand about this market.

The biggest group is leisure travellers: families going home for Diwali, couples flying to Goa, wedding guests heading to Jaipur. They book weeks ahead, they hunt for the lowest fare and they are loyal to nobody. They fill planes but they do not fill wallets. Then come business travellers, a smaller group that matters far more for profit: they book late, fly the trunk routes between Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, and pay higher fares. Their numbers follow corporate activity, IT and financial services hiring, and how many meetings have moved to video calls since 2020.

Visiting friends and relatives is a distinctively Indian tile. Millions of families have someone working in the Gulf or a big city, and they fly to see them. This drives traffic on tier-two city connections and on international routes to the Gulf and Southeast Asia, and it moves with migration, remittances and Gulf employment.

International and connecting passengers are the frontier. For decades the Gulf carriers carried Indians to Europe and America via their hubs. Now Air India is rebuilding long-haul with a new fleet and IndiGo has started flying to Europe with leased widebodies. Bilateral seat rights, negotiated government to government, decide how fast that can grow.

Cargo shippers fill the belly with pharma, electronics and perishables. Government and oil companies charter helicopters for offshore rigs, VIP movement and pilgrim routes like Kedarnath, where a helicopter crash in 2025 led to tighter oversight. And farmers, miners and utilities are the drone door's customers, paying for crop spraying and surveys, often encouraged by schemes like Namo Drone Didi, which trains women's self-help groups as drone operators.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read every tile in three lines: who buys, what they buy, what moves them.

  • Leisure travellers and visiting friends and relatives are the volume. They move with middle-class income, festival and wedding calendars, migration and remittances.
  • Business travellers are the margin. They move with corporate activity and hiring.
  • International and connecting passengers move with visas, seat rights and Gulf carrier capacity.
  • Cargo shippers move with exports, e-commerce and sea-freight disruption.
  • Government and oil companies and farmers, miners and utilities are the charter, helicopter and drone doors' customers.

Map the tiles to the doors from card one. The first five tiles belong to the airline doors. The last two belong to the charter and drone doors. That split makes it clear how differently those businesses behave: an airline lives on household spending, a helicopter operator lives on an oil company's drilling budget.

The so-what line holds the most useful insight on this card: domestic leisure is the volume and business travel is the margin. So when an airline reports full planes and low fares in the same quarter, it is telling you it was a leisure quarter, not a profitable one. Always check fares alongside load factor before celebrating a record passenger month.

c4.story:
The economics of an airline can be summed up in two numbers: how much it earns for flying one seat one kilometre, and how much it costs to do so. The industry calls them RASK and CASK, revenue and cost per available seat kilometre. Everything else is commentary.

On the revenue side, RASK is fares times fullness. A plane that is mostly full at decent fares earns well; a full plane at fire-sale fares earns little. On the cost side, the biggest single item is fuel, roughly a third of costs, moving with crude, the rupee and state taxes. Indian airlines cannot hedge it well, so it hits within a quarter. That is why analysts strip fuel out and look at CASK excluding fuel: it tells you how disciplined the airline itself is, independent of the oil price. This is the number that separates IndiGo from everyone else.

Then come the planes. Because most are leased, accounting rules turn the lease rent into depreciation and interest, making it the second-largest cost. And because those leases are in dollars, a weaker rupee creates a foreign-exchange loss on the balance sheet even if nothing operational changed. More than one IndiGo quarter has shown a strong operating result dented by a currency loss.

An airline is a business where every extra passenger is almost pure profit and every empty seat is almost pure loss.

The quirkiest line is grounding compensation. When engines are grounded for a manufacturer's defect, the engine maker compensates the airline. Since 2023 that income has been a noticeable slice of reported profit at affected carriers, which raises an uncomfortable question: how much of the profit came from flying, and how much from not flying?

Working capital, meanwhile, is a friend to the growing airline. Passengers pay weeks before they fly, so a growing airline holds customer cash. A shrinking one bleeds it, which is exactly how weak airlines have run out of money.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, for the scale low-cost airline and the sub-scale airline. Start at the left and move right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees of revenue.
  • The input bar here is fuel alone. It takes about a third for the leader and around two fifths for the sub-scale airline, which flies older, thirstier planes and has less bargaining power.
  • The opex bar is crew, airport charges, maintenance and selling. It is the biggest bar in both charts, and bigger for the sub-scale airline, which lacks the leader's scale in everything from crew rostering to maintenance contracts.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is the leased fleet. It is heavy for both, nearly a fifth for the leader.
  • The last bar is what is left. The leader keeps about a tenth. The sub-scale airline keeps almost nothing, a sliver you can barely see. That sliver is the whole story of door two.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover for the amounts.

Below, the list marks which lines matter. Five get a clear yes: revenue per seat kilometre, cost per seat kilometre excluding fuel, fuel, depreciation and lease charges, and interest with currency losses. Three get a sometimes: working capital, capex, and grounding compensation. The so-what line tells you how to read a result: the gap between revenue and cost per seat kilometre first, then how much of the profit came from compensation rather than flying.

c5.story:
Aviation demand in India grows almost every year, and yet the industry has made money in only a handful of them. How can both be true? Because profit swings not with demand but with three things the airlines barely control: crude, the rupee and how many seats everyone else adds.

The last full cycle is a lesson in all three. From 2015 to 2017 crude collapsed, fares held and passenger growth ran in the high teens. IndiGo listed in 2015 and posted its best margins. Then, as always, everyone ordered planes. By 2018 capacity was flooding in, crude was rising again and the rupee was sliding. Margins vanished. In April 2019 Jet Airways, once the country's premier private airline, stopped flying.

Then Covid grounded the entire fleet. The government capped fares and capacity for over two years. The industry lost more in that period than it had earned in a decade. In January 2022 the Tatas took back Air India after almost seven decades in state hands.

The recovery had a twist nobody planned. Travel came roaring back in 2022, Akasa launched, fare caps were lifted in August. Then, in 2023, Pratt and Whitney disclosed a manufacturing defect in its new-generation engines. Dozens of Indian planes were grounded for inspections. Go First, which flew those engines, filed for insolvency, blaming its supplier. Suddenly seats were scarce, fares rose and IndiGo posted record profits while placing the largest aircraft order in history.

The boom has had shocks: the Air India Dreamliner crash at Ahmedabad in June 2025, the Pakistan airspace closure, and in December 2025 IndiGo's own crew-scheduling crisis, when tighter pilot duty rules caught it short and thousands of flights were cancelled over a few days. But the fundamental shape holds: demand ahead of supply. The question is what happens when the grounded planes return and Air India's new fleet arrives.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock shows boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top, labelled with the last cycle: boom from 2015 to 2017, peak in 2018, bust from 2019 to 2021, bottom in 2021. Notice how long the bust lasted, three years. The arrow sits in the boom arc, labelled capacity-constrained, with the detail that fares are high and grounded planes are returning. That detail is the warning inside the boom.

The timeline runs from 2019. Two bust entries, a neutral recovery year, two boom years in 2023 and 2024, a neutral 2025 shaken by the crash and the airspace closure, and the entry marked now. Read the now entry carefully: the leader is growing internationally, the sub-scale carrier is in court, and the capacity squeeze is easing.

The four hands tell you where the boom is headed.

  • Domestic passengers: high single digits, arrow up.
  • Grounded aircraft: falling, arrow down. This looks like good news but the arrow is red for a reason: returning planes add seats, soften fares and cut compensation income.
  • Crude in rupees: elevated and steady, flat.
  • Air India and new-entrant capacity: rising, arrow down. Rival seats arriving faster than demand is how every past boom ended.

One hand up, one flat, two down. That is a boom whose supports are being removed one by one, which is exactly what the so-what line says.

c6.story:
An airline's profit is decided to a startling degree by numbers set far from any airport. The price of Brent crude in London. The dollar-rupee rate in Mumbai. The mood of the Indian middle class. Engine delivery schedules in Connecticut and Toulouse.

Three dials carry maximum weight. Crude oil comes first: fuel is about a third of costs and moves within a quarter. The dollar comes second, and it is sneakier than it looks. Leases, maintenance, spare parts and much of fuel pricing are dollar-linked, and lease liabilities on the balance sheet are revalued every quarter, so a weaker rupee raises costs and books a paper loss at once. The cruel part is that crude and the dollar tend to rise together: when oil spikes, India's import bill swells and the rupee weakens. The two biggest cost dials move the same way at the worst possible times.

The third heavy dial is demand: middle-class income and confidence, which decide whether families fly home for the holidays or take the train.

Crude and the rupee are half an airline's cost base, and they usually attack together.

Then the mixed dials. Engine and aircraft delivery delays cut both ways: they keep fares high by capping industry capacity, but they also cap the airline's own growth. That has been the defining dial of the boom since 2023. Airport charges add cost, but new terminals add capacity; the Navi Mumbai airport, which began commercial flights at the end of 2025, eases one of the tightest slot constraints in the country. Transport inflation signals pricing power but risks a political reaction: the civil aviation ministry has summoned airlines more than once over festive fare spikes.

And the quieter ones: interest rates abroad, which set lease rates, state taxes on aviation fuel, and geopolitics, which can close an airspace corridor overnight.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across: the dial, the channel, what a rise does, and the weight in dots.

  • Red downward arrows mean a rise hurts. There are many: crude, the dollar, interest rates abroad, geopolitics, and state fuel taxes.
  • Green upward arrows mean a rise helps: middle-class income and business activity, the demand dials.
  • Diamonds mean mixed: engine delays, airport charges and transport inflation.

Count the three-dot rows. There are three: crude oil, the dollar and middle-class income. Two of the three are costs the airline cannot control, and one is demand. The balance tells you that in aviation the cost side swings profit more than the demand side.

The last column shows today's reading where a series is tracked: Brent crude, the rupee, the Nifty as a proxy for confidence, the US ten-year yield for lease rates, industrial output for business activity, India VIX for geopolitical nerves, and transport inflation. Engine delays, fuel taxes and airport charges show a dash; for those, read the airline's fleet commentary and the airport regulator's orders.

The so-what line gives you the shortcut: if you track only two dials, track crude and the dollar-rupee rate. A simple habit is to look at crude priced in rupees rather than in dollars, because that combines both into one line and shows you the airline's real fuel bill.

c7.story:
Why has Indian aviation been such a graveyard when demand keeps rising? The bottlenecks tell the story, and three of them are structural.

The first is slots. Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru carry a large share of all passengers, and at peak hours their runways are full. A new entrant cannot simply buy its way in. The incumbent's bank of slots, built over years, is its real moat, more durable than any brand. When Jet Airways collapsed in 2019, its slots were redistributed, and the carriers that grabbed them, IndiGo above all, locked in an advantage.

The second is the currency mismatch. Planes, engines, spare parts and overhauls are priced in dollars; tickets are sold in rupees. The rupee's long slide over the years has acted like a permanent cost escalator. The third is fuel tax. Aviation fuel sits outside GST, and states levy VAT on it, so Indian airlines pay some of the highest fuel prices in the world. Moving it into GST has been discussed for years without happening.

Then come the cyclical and recurring bites. Engine groundings, triggered by the Pratt and Whitney defect in 2023, have kept a large share of the new-generation fleet parked in rotation, waiting months for spare engines. Pilots and crew are scarce: training a captain takes years, poaching is rife, and when the regulator tightened duty-time rules in late 2025, IndiGo's December meltdown showed how thin the margin for error had become. Safety incidents hit the whole industry: after the Ahmedabad crash in 2025, the regulator ordered fleet checks and demand dipped across carriers.

The slow one is maintenance going abroad, slowly fixing itself as Indian overhaul shops grow. And the two-sided one is political pressure on fares: tolerated in good times, capped in crises, as during Covid.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites and a severity label. The label tells you how to treat it.

  • Structural: three rows, slots at the big airports, dollar costs with rupee revenue, and aviation fuel taxes. Permanent. Notice that one of the three, slots, is actually a gift to the incumbent. The other two are why even the best airline keeps little.
  • Cyclical: engine groundings. Listed first because it is the bottleneck that created the current boom. When it eases, fares soften.
  • Recurring: pilots and crew, and safety incidents. These are the headlines that can hit any quarter, and they hit the whole industry, not just the airline involved.
  • Slow: maintenance going abroad, gradually improving as Indian overhaul capacity grows.
  • Two-sided: fare caps and political pressure. Pricing power exists in a boom, but it is tolerated, not guaranteed.

The so-what line is worth reading twice: the slot moat and the engine shortage are why one airline earns money today; the dollar and the fuel tax are why even that airline keeps so little.

A practical way to use the table: the structural rows set your long-term margin expectation, the cyclical row tells you when the current boom ends, and the recurring rows deserve a news alert. If you see a regulator audit, a crew shortage or a run of incidents, expect a soft quarter for the whole sector.

c8.story:
Aviation is one of the most regulated industries on earth, for good reason. In India the rulebook decides who can fly, where, when, at what airport cost, and occasionally at what fare.

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation is the safety regulator. It certifies planes and pilots, sets duty-time rules, licenses airlines and can ground a fleet after an incident. Its tighter pilot duty rules took full effect in late 2025, and when IndiGo's rosters could not cope, thousands of flights were cancelled in early December until the regulator granted the airline temporary relief. The ministry of civil aviation sets policy, negotiates bilateral seat rights that decide how many international flights Indian and foreign carriers can operate, and monitors fares. During Covid it capped them outright until August 2022.

The Airport Economic Regulatory Authority fixes landing, parking and passenger fees at major airports for five-year blocks. A tariff order can swing an airline's airport costs, and an airport operator's profit, for years. Slot allocation, by airport operators, decides who gets the prized peak-hour departures.

Some rules widen the market. UDAN, the regional connectivity scheme, subsidises routes to small towns with fare caps and airport fee waivers. GIFT City's tax-advantaged leasing zone is beginning to move a dollar cost line onshore. The drone rules of 2021, a production-linked incentive for drone makers and a ban on importing foreign drones in 2022 opened the drone door almost from scratch.

When lessors can repossess a plane quickly, everyone's lease gets cheaper.

The most interesting new rule is the Cape Town Convention law, passed by Parliament in April 2025. Lessors struggled for months to recover planes and engines from Go First and SpiceJet. A law that lets them repossess quickly lowers the risk premium they charge every Indian airline.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care, and status.

  • Always: four rows, the safety regulator, the civil aviation ministry, the airport tariff regulator and the airport operators. Permanent fixtures that can ground a fleet, cap fares, reset airport costs or allocate slots. Unlike many industries, these always rows make news often.
  • Live: three rows, the UDAN regional scheme, GIFT City leasing and the drone rules with their incentive scheme. These shape regional growth, leasing costs and the drone door today.
  • New: the Cape Town Convention law. It lowers lease costs across the industry and removes a weapon weak airlines once used to delay repossession, which matters for anyone holding the sub-scale airline.
  • Coming: aviation fuel taxation. The why column calls a move into GST the single biggest margin event for airlines. It has been coming for years; if it ever arrives, the whole cost structure shifts.

A good way to read the card: the always rows are risks, the live and new rows are slow tailwinds, and the one coming row is a potential jackpot. For the sub-scale airline, the Cape Town law cuts both ways: cheaper leases in principle, but lessors with sharper teeth if dues go unpaid.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Run aviation through Porter's five forces and you understand Buffett's joke in a single chart.

Start with suppliers. There are two big aircraft makers, Airbus and Boeing, a handful of engine makers and a few big lessors. They are paid first, in dollars, and they have the order backlogs to prove who holds the cards. When Pratt and Whitney's engines needed inspection, airlines waited. When Airbus delivery slots filled up years ahead, airlines queued. No airline on earth has much leverage over this group, and Indian airlines are no exception.

Buyers are hardly better. Passengers compare every fare on their phones and have no loyalty to speak of. The leader at least has a partial answer: it owns the slots passengers need at convenient times on busy routes, and its network is dense enough to offer the most choice. Rivalry is moderate for the leader, which sets fares, and brutal for the sub-scale carrier, which must match those fares with higher costs.

Entry is the interesting force. In theory, anyone with funding can lease planes and start an airline; Akasa did exactly that in 2022. In practice, slots at the big airports and a decade of cost learning cannot be bought. That is why the leader's entrant score is low while the sub-scale carrier's is higher: a new entrant takes share from the weak first.

The suppliers keep most of the money in aviation. The leader keeps a thin slice. The rest keep nothing.

Substitutes are the slow-burning threat. Video calls replaced some business trips after 2020. Vande Bharat trains compete on shorter routes, and the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail line, under construction, could eventually take a real bite out of one of the busiest city pairs.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches, the more pressure. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes: the scale low-cost airline and the sub-scale airline. Look at size first. The sub-scale shape is larger or equal on every spoke, and it reaches the outer ring on three of them. This is what a broken business looks like on a radar.

Now look for the spoke where both shapes touch the edge. It is suppliers, scored at the maximum for both. That is the most important mark on the chart: even the best airline in the country faces maximum supplier pressure. Scale buys you better terms, but not leverage.

  • Rivalry: moderate for the leader, maximum for the sub-scale carrier.
  • Buyers: moderate for the leader, which owns the slots, maximum for the sub-scale carrier.
  • Entrants: low for the leader, the smallest mark on the chart, and moderate for the sub-scale carrier.
  • Substitutes: moderate for both, a little higher for the weaker airline.

The leader's shape is not small either; it just has two short spokes, entrants and rivalry, which are exactly the slot moat and the cost advantage from earlier cards.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with a reason. The so-what line under it is the summary you can repeat at dinner: suppliers keep most of the profit, the one airline with scale keeps a thin slice, and the rest keep nothing.

c10.story:
An airline results call throws a lot at you: fleet counts, network additions, new routes, loyalty programmes. Eight numbers are enough to know whether the quarter was good and whether the next will be.

Start with load factor, how full the planes were. Above the mid-eighties is healthy for Indian domestic flying; in the nineties is pricing power. But never read it alone. Pair it with revenue per available seat kilometre, which combines fares and fullness. If load factor is high but RASK is falling, the airline filled its planes by cutting fares, which is the leisure-quarter trap from earlier.

Then the cost discipline number: cost per seat kilometre excluding fuel. This is the one that separates good airlines from bad. It should be flat or falling in rupees; rising faster than inflation is a warning that crew, maintenance or airport costs are slipping.

Next, fuel as a share of sales, your exposure to crude and the rupee. Then two margin lines. EBITDA margin shows operating profit after fuel and before the planes. Net margin shows what survives leases, interest and currency losses. Here the history is humbling: over a decade, the industry's average net margin has been close to zero.

Employee cost as a share of sales tells you about crew productivity and wage pressure. After the December 2025 scheduling crisis, more pilots per plane is likely to be a permanent feature of the cost base.

And finally, the uncomfortable one: grounded aircraft and compensation income. With planes parked by engine problems since 2023, engine makers have been compensating airlines. A profit propped up by compensation is a profit that disappears as the planes return. Falling groundings and compensation shrinking as a share of profit is the healthy direction.
c10.read:
One row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask each airline you look at.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures. Note the net margin row: it reminds you that a good year is mid-single digits and the decade average is near zero. Calibrate your expectations accordingly.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of the industry's listed companies in our database. It is shown for fuel share, EBITDA margin, net margin and employee cost.

Four rows show a dash: load factor, revenue per seat kilometre, cost per seat kilometre excluding fuel, and grounded aircraft with compensation income. These are the most important numbers on the sheet, and none of them sits in standard filings. You find them in the airline's investor presentation and the regulator's monthly traffic data.

A caution on the median column: the listed universe is tiny and mixes a scale airline, a distressed one, and charter and drone operators. A median across such different businesses tells you less than in a crowded industry. Use it as a rough backdrop and compare each company against the good mark and its own history instead. For the leader, the row to watch most closely now is the last one: how much of profit came from not flying.

c11.story:
The best clues about an airline's next quarter come from outside its results. The regulator publishes domestic passenger data every month. Crude and the rupee trade every day. Airlines and engine makers update grounding counts and delivery schedules. Hotel chains and travel portals talk about forward bookings. IT companies talk about hiring and travel budgets. And lessors talk about how tight the global aircraft market is.

Each speaks with a different lead time. Monthly passenger data and geopolitical flare-ups are this quarter: traffic is revenue immediately, and an airspace closure adds fuel and hours the same week. Crude and the rupee, grounding counts, hotel and booking commentary, and corporate hiring speak a quarter ahead. Air India's delivery schedule and lessors' commentary speak two quarters ahead, because rival seats arriving next year set the odds of the next fare war.

Combine them and you get the three-part test. The industry is in an up-cycle when passenger growth outruns seat additions, crude in rupees is flat or falling, and the balance sheet adds planes without adding debt. All three together means the rare profitable year. Two means fragile. One means a fare war is coming.

Right now two are true. Passengers are outgrowing seats, because groundings still bind. The leader is cash-rich and growing without stretching its balance sheet, while its rival is broke. The missing sign is crude in rupees, elevated with a weak rupee.

That is why the call is cautious despite the boom. It says own the leader if you own the sector at all, size the position for the fare war that has followed every Indian aviation boom, and treat the rest as rescue trades. The things to watch: crude falling sharply, which would extend the boom; rival capacity landing faster than demand; or a safety shock at the leader.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for its channel.

  • Same quarter: monthly domestic passenger data from the regulator, and geopolitical flare-ups near air corridors.
  • One quarter ahead: crude and the rupee, grounding counts and engine-maker delivery guidance, hotel and travel-portal booking commentary, and corporate hiring.
  • Two quarters ahead: Air India and new-entrant delivery schedules, and lessor and global capacity commentary. These are the earliest warnings, and they are both about supply, not demand.

That last point is the key to using this chart. The right-hand dots tell you when the boom ends, because Indian aviation booms end when seats arrive, not when passengers disappear.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs. Two ticks: passengers outgrowing seats, with groundings still binding, and growth without debt, with the leader cash-rich and the rival broke. One cross: crude in rupees is elevated and the rupee is weak. This rule is stricter than most on the page: two of three means fragile, not healthy.

The call box gives the directional view and what would change it: crude falling sharply, rival capacity arriving faster than demand, or a safety or airspace shock at the leader. Treat them as alerts, and note that the first is the only one that would make the call more positive.
